source.title: Selling the Wind
source.summary: Short-selling, futures, and the tulip mania: what medieval jurists already knew about selling what doesn't exist.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Bay' al-ma'dum: the sale of what does not exist. Islamic jurists prohibited selling fish still in the sea, crops not yet harvested, and goods you don't possess. In 1637, the Dutch were trading tulip futures at prices exceeding houses, for bulbs still in the ground. In 2008, banks were selling insurance on bonds they didn't own. This episode traces the thread from medieval Islamic contract law through the South Sea Bubble, tulip mania, and modern short-selling, showing how the prohibition on selling the non-existent was a safeguard against speculative bubbles that European markets wouldn't discover for centuries.

Fast forward to 1637: Dutch traders were selling tulip bulbs still in the ground for prices exceeding Amsterdam houses. 2008: banks were selling insurance on bonds they didn't own. The thread connecting medieval contract law to modern financial crises reveals how prohibition on selling the non-existent was designed as a safeguard against speculative bubbles.
